5 PAGES
Put the pieces together,
and the complete picture
of our reality becomes
astonishingly humbling.
Normal matter makes up
roughly 5 percent.
Dark matter claims about
27 percent.
And dark energy commands
an overwhelming 68 percent.
Together, dark matter and
dark energy make up
about 95 percent of
the total cosmic pie.
Imagine walking into an
enormous library containing
millions of books,
only to realize that
you can read merely
five pages in a
single volume, while the
rest are written in
invisible ink.
You would not say
you understood the library.
You would say you
had barely begun.
And yet, this is
not a story of defeat.
Astronomers noticed that
stars at the edge
of galaxies moved too fast.
They noticed that distant
exploding stars revealed
a speeding expansion.
They followed small oddities
in the data,
and those oddities pointed
to something enormous.
Think about how modest
the clues were.
A star turning a
little too fast.
A distant explosion looking
a little too faint.
These were numbers in
a notebook, and when
astronomers trusted the
numbers instead of the
expectations, an entire
hidden universe came into
view.
Every great discovery begins
with a clue that
does not fit.
Science does not shrink
from such surprises.
It follows them,
and in doing so,
it learns the size
of its own ignorance.
So when you step
outside tonight and look
up at the night
sky, take a quiet
breath and look past
the glowing pinpricks of
light.
The stars and galaxies
are not the main show.
They are merely tiny
specks of bright foam
floating on top of
a vast, unseen ocean.
We are conscious creatures
made of a rare,
luminous minority, striving
to decipher the dark
sea that cradles us.
So here is the summary.
We know how much
seems to be there.
We know that the
expansion is speeding up.
And we do not
know what either dark
component really is.
That is not a
failure of science.
It is where science
is doing its most
interesting work.
